extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; economists; general educated readers
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations discussing the origins of exchange, the division of labour, the limits imposed by market extent, and the origin and functions of money and value. Useful for readers studying classical political economy and foundational economic principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propensity to truck, barter, and exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Men have a natural propensity to 'truck, barter, and exchange' which leads them to obtain from one another the greater part of those good offices they need by interesting others' self-love rather than their benevolence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained with contrasts to other animals (dogs do not deliberately exchange goods) and examples (puppy fawning on dam; spaniel seeking master's attention). Emphasises that people address others' self-interest — 'Give me that which I want, and you shall have this which you want' — not their humanity. Even beggars obtain many occasional wants by purchase or barter rather than pure charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour arises from exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: The certainty of being able to exchange surplus produce for what one needs encourages individuals to apply themselves to particular occupations, cultivating talents and bringing skills to perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with a tribe of hunters/shepherds: one makes bows and arrows (armourer), another makes hut frames (house-carpenter), another a smith, etc. The ability to exchange surplus output for others' goods gives incentive to specialize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference of talents is largely the effect of division of labour
rubrics_metrics.description: The remarkable difference of genius between professions (e.g., philosopher vs street porter) arises more from habit, custom, and education due to their different employments than from nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues children may be similar at birth but are shaped by divergent occupations; the specialisation widens perceived differences in talent and character over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour is limited by the extent of the market
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which labour can be divided and specialization encouraged is always limited by the extent of the market (the power of exchanging). When the market is small, there is little encouragement to dedicate oneself entirely to one employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a porter needs a large town; in remote rural areas farmers must perform many tasks themselves; absence of a sufficient market makes specialized trades (e.g., nailer) unsustainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport and communication (especially water-carriage) expand the market and enable specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements in means of carriage, particularly water-carriage, open more extensive markets and thereby naturally cause industry to subdivide and improve sooner along coasts and navigable rivers than inland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed comparison: land waggons vs ships between London and Edinburgh (six–eight men on a ship can move as much as 50 waggons and many horses over same time), showing lower labour and animal maintenance costs for water transport. Historical/geographical examples: Mediterranean coastal civilizations, Egypt with Nile canals, Bengal and eastern China with river branches and inland navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of money as remedy for the coincidence of wants
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct barter fails because parties do not have mutually wanted goods, people prudently keep some commonly acceptable commodity to facilitate exchange; this practice gave rise to money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples of things used as media of exchange: cattle, salt, shells, dried cod, tobacco, sugar, hides, and nails. The passage emphasises the pragmatic search for commodities 'few people would be likely to refuse in exchange.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Metals preferred for money because of durability and divisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Metals were eventually preferred as the medium of commerce because they are least perishable and can be divided into any number of parts and re-united by fusion, qualities making them especially fit as instruments of commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison with other media: cattle require buying in large lumps; metals allow precise proportional exchange. Different societies used different metals historically (iron in Sparta, copper in early Rome, gold and silver among rich commercial nations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coinage (public stamp) instituted to prevent fraud and avoid weighing/assaying
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicly stamping certain quantities of metal (coinage) was necessary to prevent frauds from adulterated metals and to save the trouble of repeated weighing and assaying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before coinage, people used unstamped bars and had to weigh and assay metals (tedious and technical), leading to vulnerability to fraud. The mint's public stamp (covering both sides/edges of pieces) was meant to ascertain both fineness and, in some cases, weight, allowing coins to be received 'by tale' without weighing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denominations originally expressed weight; rulers debased coinage
rubrics_metrics.description: Coin denominations originally corresponded to the weight or quantity of metal contained; over time princes and states diminished the real quantity of metal in coins (debasement), benefiting debtors at creditors' expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical details: Roman as/pondo contained a Roman pound of copper; English pound sterling historically contained a known pound of silver. Over ages coins were reduced in metal content (examples: Roman as reduced to 1/24th of original; English pound/penny now about a third of original). Debasement allowed apparent fulfilment of obligations while defrauding creditors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value has two senses: 'value in use' and 'value in exchange'
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'value' sometimes denotes the utility of an object ('value in use') and sometimes the power of purchasing other goods that possession of that object conveys ('value in exchange'); these two can diverge (e.g., water vs diamond).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that things most useful (water) can have little exchange value, while things of little practical use (diamond) can command great exchange value; this distinction frames the study of what determines exchangeable value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour as the real measure of exchangeable value (real price)
rubrics_metrics.description: Labour is the real measure of the exchangeable value of all commodities; the real price of anything is the toil and trouble of acquiring it. Labour was 'the first price' and 'the original purchase money' paid for all things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the buyer purchases goods by labour (directly or via money/goods that embody labour). The value of a commodity to its possessor who intends to exchange it equals the quantity of labour it can command or purchase. Wealth is accordingly related to the quantity of labour one can command; the passage links real price, toil of acquisition, and the labour embodied in money or goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money's role as the universal instrument of commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: By means of money, goods of all kinds are bought and sold or exchanged for one another; money becomes in civilized nations the universal instrument of commerce enabling specialization and wider exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarises that once coined money and a circulating medium exist, exchange and specialization are greatly facilitated; money intermediates exchanges that otherwise would be hampered by the lack of coincidence of wants.
